title: The Skybridge Rescue
openingPromise: A floating city has split apart in a storm. Sky-creatures are stranded on drifting islands, and the only way across is a bridge YOU grow — plank by plank — by commanding equal groups. Multiplication is not the quiz here; it is the crane, the winch, and the bridge itself.
firstThreeSeconds: The screen opens already in the world: a broken bridge gap glowing at center, a small creature waving from the far island, and one giant pulsing button reading "GROW BRIDGE." A single plank-bundle (a visible group of planks) sits beside the gap. No menus, no settings, no tutorial wall. The camera drifts gently toward the gap so the child's eye lands exactly where the action is.
firstAction: Tap the pulsing GROW BRIDGE button. One bundle of 4 planks visibly slots into the gap with a satisfying clunk — the child immediately sees that one action = one equal group added. The gap shows it still needs more, and a counter appears: "Gap needs 12 planks. Each bundle holds 4. How many bundles?" The child taps a number from a big three-choice arc (2, 3, 4). No typing, no dragging required to start.
coreInteraction: Every obstacle in the sky-city is repaired by choosing HOW MANY equal groups of a given size to deploy — bundles of planks, crates of rivets, teams of wind-gliders, coils of rope. The child reads the situation (total needed, group size shown physically in the world), then commands the number of groups. The world executes the command literally: choose 3 bundles of 4 and the crane swings exactly 3 times, dropping 4 planks each swing, while a running tally climbs 4, 8, 12. Correct commands complete structures; the reasoning is visible as motion. Each mission reframes equal-groups in an unfamiliar surface context (rope strands per anchor, gliders per stranded creature, lantern-fuel cells per beacon) so the child must transfer the construct, not repeat a drilled format. Item contexts are freshly authored and never reuse the exposed baseline items (no 3-by-4 array, no 5-by-2 equal-groups framing).
mathAsPower: Multiplication is literally the child's superpower verb. The child never "answers a question and then watches a reward" — the number they choose IS the command the machines obey. Too few groups and the bridge visibly stops short over the void; too many and the crane over-swings and planks tumble off the edge. The exact product is the only thing that makes the world hold together. Understanding equal groups = controlling the world.
stakes: Stranded sky-creatures stand on shrinking cloud-islands that slowly drift apart. Each mission has a visible, gentle urgency: the creature paces, the island edge crumbles softly, wind picks up. Nothing terrifying — no death, no timers screaming — but the world makes clear that the bridge matters to someone who is waiting on the child.
consequences: Wrong group counts play out physically and legibly. Choose 2 bundles when 3 are needed: the bridge extends, the creature steps out hopefully, reaches the end, and points at the remaining gap while the tally reads 8 of 12. Choose 4 bundles: the extra swing dumps planks into the clouds below with a comic bloop, and the tally reads 16 of 12 with the surplus highlighted. The consequence always teaches: the child SEES exactly how far off they were and in which direction, in units of the group size.
recovery: No fail screens, no lives. After a miss, the world offers a one-tap "Count the swings" replay: the crane re-runs the child's own command in slow motion with the running tally (4... 8...) so they can see where it landed relative to the target, then hands control straight back for another command. Materials are never lost permanently — spilled planks are winched back up. Because the evidence contract is unseen transfer (practice cannot establish mastery), retried items are marked internally as assisted attempts; recovery protects the child's momentum without inflating the evidence record.
progression: Mission 1 — The First Gap: single bridge span, group size shown as a physical bundle, three-choice arc for number of groups, running tally always visible. Establishes the verb: groups-of-N close gaps.

Mission 2 — The Rope Anchors: unfamiliar surface (each anchor post needs an equal number of rope strands; total strands given). Same one-command interaction, but the child must recognize the equal-groups structure themselves — nothing says 'multiply.' Choice arc widens to five options.

Mission 3 — The Glider Lift: inverted framing (you know the number of groups of gliders and how many creatures each glider carries; will everyone fit across?). Child now commands group SIZE instead of group count, transferring the construct across roles.

Mission 4 — The Beacon Relay: two-step transfer under gentle wind pressure — fuel cells per lantern, lanterns per tower — where the child sequences two equal-groups commands to light the way. The tally scaffold fades unless summoned.

Final Mission — The Grand Span: one fresh, unseen scenario combining a novel context and quantity range never practiced, serving as the clean transfer evidence moment. No hints active; the world simply waits for the command.
worldReaction: The sky-city keeps score in scenery, not points. Every solved mission permanently changes the skyline: bridges stay built, rescued creatures move into view and wave when the camera passes, lanterns the child lit keep glowing, wind-chimes made of recovered planks ring softly. Precise commands (right on the first try) earn a golden rivet visibly hammered into that bridge — the city itself becomes a record of the child's reasoning.
payoff: When the Grand Span completes, all rescued creatures cross at once in a procession over every bridge the child built, the camera pulling back to reveal the whole reconnected city — each span labeled with the equal-groups command that built it (e.g., '6 groups of 3'). The final shot is the child's multiplication written into the architecture. A short 'Bridgewright' badge moment names what they proved: they used equal groups somewhere they had never seen them before.
replayVariation: On replay, the storm scatters the city differently: gap totals, group sizes, and surface contexts are regenerated from fresh item pools (never the exposed baseline items, never a verbatim repeat of a prior run). Mission order of the middle contexts shuffles, and one wildcard context (e.g., seed-pods per sky-garden planter) appears per run so transfer stays genuinely unseen. Golden rivets from prior runs remain visible as history, inviting a cleaner run rather than the same run.
visualDirection: Warm painterly skies at golden hour: soft coral clouds, teal-and-cream floating islands, wooden machinery with brass fittings. High-contrast readability — the gap, the group bundle, and the command button are the three brightest things on screen at all times. Numbers appear as physical objects (stamped on crates, carved into planks), never as floating UI where a world object could carry them. Interface chrome is nearly zero; the world is the interface.
motionDirection: Motion always narrates the math. Groups deploy one at a time with a clear rhythmic cadence — swing, drop, tally tick — never as an instant sum. Camera moves are slow and purposeful: drift to the gap on mission start, gentle push-in as the last group lands, wide pull-back on completion. Wrong-answer physics are soft and comic (planks bounce, flutter, bloop into clouds), never harsh. Idle world breathes: clouds drift, creatures fidget, chimes sway, so waiting never feels frozen.
soundDirection: A gentle wind-and-wood ambience underneath everything. Each group deployment gets an ascending marimba note, so 3 groups of 4 literally sounds like a rising three-note phrase — the child can HEAR the count of groups. Exact completion resolves the phrase with a warm chord and creature cheer; undershoot ends on an unresolved note (musically 'not there yet'); overshoot adds a comic slide-whistle plank-tumble. No buzzer sounds, no failure stingers. The Grand Span finale layers every mission's motif into one melody.
usefulLibraries: Pixi.js or plain Canvas 2D for layered parallax sky rendering
GSAP or Web Animations API for crane-swing and tally choreography
Howler.js for layered ambient audio and pitched deployment notes
A tiny seeded-PRNG utility for reproducible-but-fresh item generation across replays
